funding: The Free State of Bavaria and the Friends of Haus der Kunst are shareholders. The Alexander Tutsek Foundation is the major supporter. The Kai and Beisheim foundations also give.
note: Graded on present funders, since the museum still exists. A Bavarian ministry official chairs its supervisory board. 2024 attendance was nearly 440,000.

propaganda.summary: Hitler had the building erected and opened it on 18 July 1937 for the annual Great German Art Exhibitions, held to 1944. His photographer Heinrich Hoffmann took charge of selecting works, and Hitler decided finally.

reason: The museum's own history page calls the Haus der Deutschen Kunst a central venue of Nazi art policy and propaganda, and the GHI source records Hitler's speech and Hoffmann replacing the jury. Fixed the summary: sources show Hoffmann led selection from 1937 with Hitler deciding, not that he directed the shows until 1944. Funding cut to 30 words. S holds: attendance about 440,000 and no budget figure over $20M found; coordinates match Nominatim.

funding: Closed 1990. The GDR state owned it and the last GDR government's Council of Ministers dissolved it. Its holdings and the Zeughaus passed to the Deutsches Historisches Museum.
note: Graded on its last owner, the GDR state, because the museum closed. The Zeughaus on Unter den Linden now houses the Deutsches Historisches Museum.

propaganda.summary: The SED Politburo decided in 1950 to found the GDR's central history museum, and the Central Committee approved its staff. It presented a Marxist-Leninist view of history that legitimised the GDR until 1990.

reason: The Federal Agency for Civic Education article records the SED Politburo decision (Feb 1950), Central Committee approval of every staff post, Politburo correction of the exhibition and the GDR government's 1990 dissolution; DHM pages confirm the mandate. Fixed the summary: the 1950 decision was the Politburo's and the SED-membership rule no longer rests on Wikipedia. Keep A: the GDR state is the last owner and state money alone is no flag. S holds; coordinates match the Zeughaus.

funding: Closed in 1993 by order of the Russian president. The State Historical Museum, a federal museum, took over the collection and the building on Revolution Square.
note: Graded on its last owner, the Russian state, because the museum closed. Part of the building now holds the 1812 Patriotic War museum.

propaganda.summary: Created in 1935 and opened in 1936, the Central Lenin Museum housed the Lenin cult under the Communist Party. Its first exhibit showed Stalin close to Lenin, and Stalin was cut after 1956.

reason: The successor museum's site says the museum showed Soviet loyalty to Lenin's cause and the Party, and the Moscow Times says it housed the Lenin cult, skewed its first exhibit toward Stalin and was cleansed after Khrushchev's 1956 speech. Dropped the unsourced 'party leadership ordered it' clause: the 1935 Politburo decree appears only on Russian Wikipedia. The row meets the bar on two sources but no scholarly work; answer to the question: keep. The 'Part of the building' note rests on the Moscow Times and ru.wikipedia.

n: State Museum of the History of Religion
funding: Federal state museum under the Russian Ministry of Culture since 1991. It moved from Kazan Cathedral to Pochtamtskaya Street 14 in 2000.
note: Graded on present funders, since the museum still exists in a different form. Its antireligious displays ended in the 1990s.

propaganda.summary: The USSR Ministry of Culture took over the museum in 1961. Its directors from 1968 to 1987, trained at the Party's atheism institute, built an atheist propaganda programme of lectures and touring exhibitions.

reason: Historian Heather Coleman's entry (scholarly, citing Shakhnovich and Chumakova and Smolkin) says the museum shifted to atheist propaganda after the 1961 move to the Ministry of Culture, with directors trained at the Central Committee's atheism institute, but that before that it stood on a blurred line between scholarship and the regime. So narrowed the period from 1932 to 1961 onward and dropped the Kazan Cathedral Wikipedia source. Answer: keep as a 1961 to 1990 row. Own site confirms founding and the ministry logo, not the atheist role.

funding: The Humanitarian Projects Foundation runs it and gets most of its money from Gazprom, per RFE/RL in 2019. Gazprom co-financed parks from 2016. Federal and Moscow bodies are partners.
note: Archimandrite Tikhon Shevkunov heads the foundation's expert council. The Education Ministry recommended the parks as teaching material in 2017.

propaganda.summary: A foundation funded mainly by Gazprom, with the presidential administration as partner, runs the parks. Historian Ivan Kurilla calls them an ideological tool, and Bumaga reported pro-war exhibits in 2023.

reason: Kurilla (PONARS Eurasia), RFE/RL and Bumaga meet the bar and Bumaga's 2023 pro-war exhibits are documented. Answer: add Fossil fuels (tier X): RFE/RL says the foundation gets most of its money from Gazprom, Gazprom's 2019 report confirms co-financing since 2016, and Bumaga documents Gazprom money through 2018 to 2021 and Gazprom Neft gifts in 2019 and 2021, within five years; no Sanctions flag since only Gazprom Neft is listed and its gift went to a related fund. L is kept on RFE/RL's 5.5 million network visits and 10 billion rubles spent, not a Moscow-only figure. Funding kept the 2019 date because no later foundation-level figure was opened. The summary now says ideological tool, Kurilla's term, not propaganda.

funding: Azerbaijani state project. President Ilham Aliyev ordered it built in January 2021 and opened it on 12 April 2021, according to the presidential website.
note: The Council of Europe human rights commissioner, the European Parliament and Armenia objected. Wax figures and helmets left the main display in October 2021.

propaganda.summary: President Ilham Aliyev proposed and opened the park, and his website says it shows the victory and Armenian war crimes. Until October 2021 it displayed wax figures of Armenian soldiers.

reason: The presidential site states Aliyev's initiative, opening and purpose (the state's own claim), the Council of Europe commissioner's letter calls the mannequins humiliating and says such displays can deepen hostility, and RFE/RL quotes an analyst calling it a spectacle to keep society mobilised; mechanism changed to founded to promote since the president built it for the victory. Protest or boycott holds: the commissioner's published letter is aimed at the president, and OC Media records the European Parliament condemnation (the call to close it rests on Wikipedia, so the note says objected). 'State project' replaces the unconfirmed 'Azerbaijani state' funder because no page names the operator or budget. Answer: keep S and the flag. Ruling of 26 October 2026: a protest older than about five years is a note, not a flag. The protests date from April 2021, so the flag is removed and the tier is U (operator and budget unnamed).

n: Museum of the Communist Party of China
funding: Built on a 2017 Communist Party Central Committee decision, with support from the National Development and Reform Commission, Finance Ministry and Beijing city. Entry is free.
note: Opened 18 June 2021. Xinhua reported more than 3.5 million visits by 30 June 2024.

propaganda.summary: The Party Central Committee decided in 2017 to build it. People's Daily, the Party paper, reports the Central Propaganda Department led construction. Xi Jinping called it a spiritual home for Party members, China Daily reports.

reason: Kept as a Party museum founded to promote the Party: China Daily (state media) gives the 2017 Central Committee decision, Xi's brief and his February 2021 plan review, People's Daily (Party paper) gives the Central Propaganda Department's leading group, and Koryo Tours describes it as dedicated to the Party's triumphs. Fixed: the managing-body claim rests on Wikipedia alone, so I cut it from funding and the summary; answer to the question: keep without it.

funding: Funded by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism as a level-1 public welfare institution. The Art Newspaper counted 7.4 million visitors in 2019.
note: Formed 2003 by merging the Museum of the Chinese Revolution and the National Museum of Chinese History. Building opened 1959.

propaganda.summary: Reviewing Denton's study, Joseph Allen says official ideology has driven Chinese museums since 1949. Time found the 2011 Road to Rejuvenation display sanitized and pro-government. Xi Jinping gave his Chinese Dream speech there in 2012.

reason: Kept, with Wikipedia replaced as the use source by Allen's MCLC review (2015) of Denton's Exhibiting the Past, plus Time (2011) and Denton's caption placing Xi's 29 November 2012 speech here. Ministry funding rests on Wikipedia alone; answer to the question: Time plus the Allen review meets the bar for the ideology line, but I found no source on Ministry control of exhibit text.

funding: Founded 1985 by the Nanjing Municipal Government; the Jiangsu provincial government added a research institute in 2016. The Standard reported about 6 million visitors in 2025.
note: The Victory Exhibition Hall opened 7 December 2015. Admission is free with prior registration.

propaganda.summary: The Nanjing municipal government built it in 1985. Emily Matson (Wilson Center) finds its phases track the Communist Party's changing legitimizing narrative. Contested Histories reports state-defined aims, including patriotic education.

reason: Kept as a today row on two independent sources: Matson (Wilson Center, 2024) and the Contested Histories case study (state-defined aims, Ministry of National Defence on patriotic education, Party-led resistance emphasis). The massacre is real; the row marks the Party's use of the hall. Fixed: coordinates were about 700 m off and now sit on the OSM building; I cut the 1996 compulsory-visits line (one passing sentence in a Foreign Policy column).

n: Museum of the War of Chinese People's Resistance Against Japanese Aggression
funding: Budget unit in the Beijing government's published accounts: 809 million yuan of public funding in 2025, 711 million of it project spending.
note: Inside Wanping Fortress near the Marco Polo Bridge. Beijing opened a patriotic education base there for Hong Kong and Macau youth in August 2025.

propaganda.summary: Mitter (China Quarterly, 2000) says Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin and Hu Qiaomu authorized it and that it shapes official memory legitimizing Party rule. A patriotic education base for Hong Kong youth opened there in 2025.

reason: Kept and upgraded. I opened Mitter's 2000 China Quarterly note in full: it says the museum shapes official memory that legitimizes CCP rule and names the leaders who authorized it. Beijing's published 2025 accounts list the museum as a budget unit (809.3 million yuan public funding, 711.1 million of it project spending), so tier U becomes A and size S becomes L; the accounts name no supervising ministry.

funding: Run under county-level administration since 1984. Provincial permission was needed for exhibit changes in 1988 (Ho and Li, Modern China, 2016).
note: The 114 clay figures were made in 1965 by Sichuan Fine Arts Institute artists. Tens of millions visited in the Mao era.

propaganda.summary: Opened in 1959 as an exhibit of the landlord's crimes. Ho and Li report officials fabricated evidence such as a water dungeon, and denounced class enemies faced show trials there in the Cultural Revolution.

reason: Fixed. The pin is the manor museum, so the row now covers the museum, sourced to Ho and Li (Modern China, 2016, peer reviewed): museum since 1959, fabricated exhibits, show trials in the Cultural Revolution, visitors fell after 1978. Start year is 1959 (not 1965) and end year 1978 (not 1976, which the study does not give). The old funding line was not about funding; the current operator stays unconfirmed, so tier stays U.

funding: Run by Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, which lists it among its institutions. Foreign adults pay $5 and Cambodians enter free, the museum states.
note: Former Khmer Rouge prison S-21. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 as part of the Cambodian Memorial Sites.

propaganda.summary: Vietnamese authorities appointed Mai Lam to turn S-21 into a museum in 1979. Rachel Hughes finds the Kampuchean Ministry of Culture, Information and Propaganda oversaw it and used foreign visits to support the regime's legitimacy.

reason: Kept with a stronger source: Hughes (Melbourne, 2018) shows the PRK Ministry of Culture, Information and Propaganda oversaw the museum and used visits to support the regime's legitimacy; Hopkins and Lowrie back Mai Lam's Vietnamese appointment. Period ends 1982 because that is what Hughes covers; no source opened dates the end of the use. Answer: keep as historical; Hopkins's claim of CPP use today is one essay, so no today row. Funding fixed to the museum site's $5 fee.

n: National Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Holy Defense
funding: Tehran municipality built it, and its statute makes the municipality responsible for the budget and staff. The museum reported about 300,000 visitors a year (AFP, 2018).
note: Opened in 2012 in Tehran's Abbas-Abad cultural district. The Armed Forces General Staff published its statute amendments in 2021.

propaganda.summary: The Tehran municipality built it. Its statute was amended in 2021 with Supreme Leader Khamenei's approval and published by the Armed Forces General Staff. AFP reported that it glorifies the Iran-Iraq war.

reason: Kept; tier U becomes A. The statute amendment (General Staff letter, Official Gazette no. 22214, 24 June 2021, read on a legal portal) makes the municipality fund the budget and staff and records Khamenei's approval; Radio Farda (2023) says the municipality paid for the project. No source opened shows IRGC funding, so the Sanctions question does not arise (and a city funder never takes that flag). Rivetti's IJMES footnote is the scholarly support; her full text was not open to me.

n: Victory Museum (Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War)
funding: The museum is a federal state budgetary cultural institution, the Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War 1941 to 1945, run by the Russian state with the Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation as its parent body. Its general director is Alexander Shkolnik, who was honoured by Putin in 2021 for patriotic education and sanctioned by the UK and Australia in 2022. The museum describes itself as a centre of patriotic education for new generations and for countering falsification of history.
note: Opened on Poklonnaya Hill on 9 May 1995 in a building by Anatoly Polyansky with 14,143 square metres of permanent galleries; the 2022 exhibition Ordinary Nazism drew 150,000 visitors in its first month.

propaganda.summary: Since April 2022 the federal museum has staged exhibitions such as Ordinary Nazism and Ordinary NATOzism presenting Ukraine's army as heirs of wartime Nazi collaborators, echoing the Kremlin's denazification justification for the invasion.

funding: Patriot Park is the Central Military-Patriotic Park of Culture and Recreation of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation, built and funded by the Russian Defence Ministry, which allocated more than 20 billion rubles to it in 2015. It covers 5,414 hectares including a 3,530 hectare military base and hosts the ministry's annual Army forum. Its head Vyacheslav Akhmedov was arrested for fraud in August 2024 together with a Defence Ministry general.
note: Conceived by Defence Minister Sergei Shoigu and opened in stages from 2015 to 2016; Putin called it a major component of the system of military-patriotic education for young people.

propaganda.summary: The Defence Ministry created the park in 2015 for military-patriotic education of youth; in August 2023 it displayed Western armoured vehicles captured in Ukraine during the Army-2023 forum, inspected by Dmitry Medvedev.

funding: From 2002 to 2026 the museum was run by the Foundation for Research on Central and Eastern European History and Society, a public foundation chaired by Mária Schmidt and financed by the Hungarian government, which gave it 5.5 billion forints in 2019. On 1 September 2026 the foundation was dissolved and its tasks passed to Kulturális Vagyonkezelő Kft, a company under the Ministry for Social Relations and Culture. Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr dismissed Schmidt on 15 September 2026 and ordered a content review of the exhibition.
note: Housed at Andrássy út 60, the former Arrow Cross and ÁVH headquarters; the museum drew millions of visitors over 24 years and is the Hungarian public collection most visited by foreigners.

propaganda.summary: The first Orbán government opened it on 24 February 2002 under Orbán's adviser Mária Schmidt; historians criticised its equation of fascism and communism and its casting of Hungary as a victim of foreign occupiers.

n: Museum of the Second World War
funding: The museum is a state cultural institution supervised and financed by Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, which appoints its director. The culture minister dismissed the PiS-appointed director Grzegorz Berendt in March 2024 and appointed Rafał Wnuk, a co-author of the original exhibition. The museum merged with the Westerplatte Museum in 2017 on the order of Culture Minister Piotr Gliński.
note: Opened 23 March 2017 in a 23,000 square metre building with a 40 metre leaning tower by the Kwadrat studio; 601,000 visitors in 2024.

propaganda.summary: In April 2017 the PiS government merged the museum, dismissed director Paweł Machcewicz and installed Karol Nawrocki, who altered the exhibition; from June 2024 the new management reversed those changes, restoring the authors' original vision.

funding: The museum is a public institution of the Ho Chi Minh City government, belonging to the city's Department of Culture and Sports. It is owned by the Vietnamese state and funded from the city budget and ticket income. It has received more than 25 million visitors in 50 years, about 500,000 a year, two thirds of them foreigners.
note: Opened 4 September 1975 at 28 Võ Văn Tần; one in six international visitors to the city tours it.

propaganda.summary: Opened by the new communist authorities on 4 September 1975 as the Exhibition House for US and Puppet Crimes, renamed in 1990 and 1995; anthropologist Christina Schwenkel describes its uncontextualised self-representation of American war crimes.

funding: The museum is a public service unit directly under Vietnam's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, with its functions set by ministerial Decision 2372/QD-BVHTTDL of 2025. The decision assigns it propaganda and education work on Ho Chi Minh's life, thought and revolutionary ethics, and it manages state-assigned finances and assets and collects fees. It has received more than 40 million visitors, over 10 million of them foreign.
note: Founded by a Party Secretariat resolution of 25 November 1970 and opened 19 May 1990 on Ho Chi Minh's centenary in a lotus-shaped building by Soviet architect Garon Isacovich; holds 130,000 documents and artefacts.

propaganda.summary: Created by Communist Party resolutions of 1970 and 1977 and opened in 1990, the state museum is tasked by ministerial decision with propaganda and education on Ho Chi Minh's thought and revolutionary ideals.

funding: The museum is owned and operated by Kültür A.Ş., the culture company of the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality, which began construction in 2005 and opened it in January 2009. It is financed by the municipality through Kültür A.Ş. and by ticket sales. Posocco describes it as one of Istanbul's most popular attractions for domestic and foreign tourists.
note: Built at Topkapı beside the point where the Ottomans breached the walls in 1453; opened with praise from Prime Minister Erdoğan after three years of construction.

propaganda.summary: The AKP-run Istanbul municipality's Kültür A.Ş. opened it in 2009 to convey the spirit of the 1453 conquest; Posocco (2018) analyses it as a case of AKP-era museums promoting Ottoman and Islamic nationalism.

funding: The museum is maintained by Yasukuni Shrine, which has been a private religious corporation since 1946 after the Occupation's Shinto Directive abolished state sponsorship of Shinto. The shrine funds it from its own resources and admission fees; it receives no government money. The revamped museum reopened in July 1986.
note: Japan's first Western-style museum, opened February 1882 on the shrine grounds; scholars criticise its revisionist account that omits the experiences of China and Korea.

propaganda.summary: Established in 1882 under the Imperial Army and made a state institution of the Army Ministry by imperial decree in 1910, it ran national spiritual mobilisation exhibitions in the 1930s until September 1945.

funding: The building is owned by Roma Capitale, the City of Rome, and run by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo, a municipal instrumental body founded in 1998 that operates under an annual service contract with the city. Palaexpo also manages the Scuderie del Quirinale and Casa del Jazz and reports one of the highest self-financing rates among Italian cultural bodies. The city's Office for Education and Culture oversees it.
note: Opened 1883 on Via Nazionale to a design by Pio Piacentini; reopened in 2007 after restoration.

propaganda.summary: The National Fascist Party under Dino Alfieri staged the Mostra della Rivoluzione Fascista here from 28 October 1932, opened by Mussolini, behind a fasces facade by Libera and De Renzi; nearly four million people attended.

funding: The hall is run by the National Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall Management Office, an agency of Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, and funded from the central government budget. The Ministry of Culture directs its transformation under the government's transitional justice policy and negotiated the 2024 honour guard change with the Ministry of National Defense. The honour guard itself is provided by the military.
note: Construction began 31 October 1976 and the hall opened 5 April 1980 with a 6.3 metre bronze statue of Chiang; the changing of the guard is a major tourist attraction.

propaganda.summary: Built 1976 to 1980 to commemorate Chiang Kai-shek with a giant statue and military honour guard; the Ministry of Culture began a transitional justice project in 2017 and removed the guard in 2024.

funding: The site is owned by the Venezuelan state and controlled by the Ministry of Defense and the Bolivarian National Militia, whose headquarters have been there since 2008. The government organises the visits and the Presidential Honour Guard guards the sarcophagus; the staging of the mausoleum was the responsibility of the state. Since 1981 it has had museum status as the Military History Museum.
note: Built 1904 to 1906 in the 23 de Enero district; by 2014 it received about 800 visitors a day and 2,000 at weekends, and acting president Delcy Rodríguez renewed her oath at the tomb on 6 January 2026 after Maduro's capture.

propaganda.summary: After Chávez died in March 2013 the Maduro government turned the barracks of his 1992 coup into his mausoleum and museum, with honour guard, daily cannon salute and state-staged narrative placing him beside Bolívar.

n: National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War
funding: The museum is a Ukrainian state museum with national status granted by presidential decree on 21 June 1996, financed from the state budget under the Ministry of Culture, which renamed it in July 2015 under the decommunisation laws and reports on its decolonisation work. Its director general is Yurii Savchuk. In 2023 the museum replaced the Soviet emblem on the Motherland Monument's shield with the Ukrainian trident.
note: The 102 metre Motherland Monument houses the main exhibition on an 11 hectare site; more than 21 million visitors since 1981.

propaganda.summary: Opened in 1981 by Leonid Brezhnev as the Ukrainian State Museum of the History of the Great Patriotic War, beneath a Motherland statue bearing the Soviet emblem, to commemorate the Soviet war narrative.

funding: The museum is run by the Stiftung Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, a non-profit foundation under civil law funded by annual matching contributions from the Free State of Saxony and the City of Dresden, with further grants from federal bodies, businesses and foundations. Its board of trustees is chaired by Dresden mayor Annekatrin Klepsch with Saxon state minister Barbara Klepsch as deputy. Iris Edenheiser has been director since 2022.
note: Founded 1912 by Odol manufacturer Karl August Lingner; about 220,000 visitors in 2004.

propaganda.summary: From 1933 the museum served Nazi racial ideology as a propaganda machine of racial hygiene, co-producing with NSDAP offices the touring exhibitions Blut und Rasse (1935 to 1938) and Ewiges Volk (1937 to 1939).
